chapters.title: Numbers, quantities, units and dimensions
chapters.what: A physical quantity is a number times a unit. Its dimension (length, mass, time …) is what survives when the unit is changed, so an equation must have the same dimension on both sides.
maths: \Pi\text{-theorem: } n \text{ quantities, } k \text{ dimensions} \Rightarrow n-k \text{ groups}
chapters.looks: On a logarithmic line equal steps are equal ratios, so a proton and a galaxy fit on one picture; a power law y = C x^n becomes a straight line whose slope is n.
chapters.change: Move a measurement and watch the fitted exponent: a physical law pins it (½ for a pendulum, ⅖ for a blast wave), noise only wobbles it.
chapters.use: Checking formulas, scaling models (wind tunnels, ship tanks), estimating the unknown (Taylor's bomb yield), unit conversions that sink spacecraft when they go wrong.
misc: Units are not decoration: 1 lbf·s ≠ 1 N·s.
A dimensionless formula can still be wrong by a pure number C — dimensions cannot find C.

examples.title: From a proton to a light-year: powers of ten
examples.world: SI prefixes (femto … peta) name these orders of magnitude.

examples.title: Pendulum period from dimensions alone: T ∝ √(L/g)
examples.world: Clock design; the 3D surface shows the same pendulum on the Moon (g = 1.62) and Jupiter (24.8).

examples.title: G. I. Taylor's Trinity estimate: R ∝ t^(2/5)
examples.world: From photographs of the 1945 fireball alone, Taylor estimated the yield — a dimensional argument, R = C (E t²/ρ)^(1/5).
examples.note: Radius–time values as tabulated in Taylor (1950, part II), measured from the Trinity film.

examples.title: Kepler's third law: T² ∝ a³ for the eight planets
examples.world: Orbit design: once one period is known, every other follows from the semi-major axis.

examples.title: Kleiber's law: metabolic rate ∝ M^(3/4)
examples.world: Drug dosing between species and the energy budgets of animals scale with this exponent, not with M.
examples.note: Points lie on Kleiber's curve B = 70 M^0.75 (mouse → elephant); the fit recovers the exponent.

examples.title: Scalars and vectors: airspeed plus wind is ground speed
examples.world: The pilot's wind triangle: heading north at 120 kn in a 30 kn wind blowing toward the east.

chapters.title: Algebra: expressions, equations, inequalities
chapters.what: An equation asks where two expressions agree; an inequality asks where one stays below another. Systems of equations meet at points; systems of inequalities carve out regions.
chapters.looks: A root is where a graph crosses a line; a linear inequality shades a half-plane; the best point of a linear programme sits at a corner of the shaded polygon.
chapters.change: Slide a constraint and the optimum jumps from corner to corner; perturb a right-hand side and an ill-conditioned system's answer swings wildly.
chapters.use: Stopping distances, production planning, circuit currents, design envelopes, growth forecasts.
misc: Squaring both sides can add false roots.
A linear programme's optimum is never strictly inside the region (unless the objective is flat).

examples.title: Stopping distance is quadratic in speed
examples.world: UK Highway Code: 96 m at 70 mph (31.3 m/s) = 21 m thinking + 75 m braking.

examples.title: Linear programming: plan production for the most profit
examples.world: The simplex method was built for exactly this (Dantzig); Stigler's 1945 diet problem is the classic.

examples.title: Loop currents of a two-loop circuit
examples.world: Mesh analysis: (R1+R2) I1 − R2 I2 = V1 and −R2 I1 + (R2+R3) I2 = −V2 with 2, 4, 6 Ω, 12 V and 6 V.

examples.title: An ill-conditioned system: a tiny change, a huge swing
examples.world: Why engineers check the condition number before trusting a solve.

examples.title: A beam design envelope from inequalities
examples.world: Allowable bending stress, a depth-to-width limit and a minimum width bound the feasible cross-sections b × h.
examples.note: Maximising −(b h) finds the lightest section; stress written as 6M/(b h²) ≤ σ_allow with M/σ_allow = a.

examples.title: Exponential growth: Moore's law doubling every two years
examples.world: Transistors per chip roughly doubled every 2 years for decades; 10 years = 5 doublings = ×32.

chapters.title: Functions and their transformations
chapters.what: A function assigns one output to each input. Shifting, stretching and reflecting its graph are themselves functions applied before or after it: y = a f(k(x − c)) + b.
chapters.looks: a stretches vertically, k squeezes horizontally, c slides right, b lifts; the 3D view stacks the whole family y = f(x; a) as a surface.
chapters.change: Sweep a from a0 to a1 (▶) and watch one slice of the family surface sweep through it.
chapters.use: Decay and dating, growth and saturation, material laws, tides, signal models.
misc: f(x − c) moves the graph RIGHT by c.
e^{−λt} never reaches zero; the half-life is the same at every age.

examples.title: The four moves: y = a sin(k(x − c)) + b
examples.world: Every sinusoidal signal (sound, AC, tides) is one of these.

examples.title: Radiocarbon decay: half left after 5730 years
examples.world: Radiocarbon dating (Arnold & Libby 1949); the Cambridge half-life 5730 ± 40 y (Godwin 1962).

examples.title: Logistic growth levels off
examples.world: Pearl & Reed fitted a logistic curve to the US census 1790-1910; epidemics and markets saturate the same way.
examples.note: t in years after 1790, P as a fraction of the carrying capacity K: the steepest growth (the tangent) is at the midpoint, P = K/2.

examples.title: Inverse-square law: light intensity 1/r²
examples.world: Double the distance from a lamp, a quarter of the light — also gravity and radiation dose.

examples.title: A piecewise function: steel's elastic–plastic stress–strain
examples.world: σ = min(E ε, σ_y) with E = 200 GPa and σ_y = 250 MPa for structural steel (idealised).

examples.title: Tides: a 12.42-hour cosine
examples.world: The principal lunar semidiurnal tide M2 has a period of 12.42 hours.

chapters.title: Analytic geometry: coordinates, conics, curves in space
chapters.what: Curves and surfaces become equations in coordinates. Circles, ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas are all one family: the points whose distance to a focus is e times their distance to a line.
chapters.looks: In 2D the conic is traced around its focus; in 3D the same curve is where a tilted plane slices a double cone.
chapters.change: Sweep e from 0 to 2: circle → ellipse → parabola (e = 1, the plane parallel to the cone's side) → hyperbola.
chapters.use: Orbits, reflectors and dishes, lithotripters, DNA and springs (helices), cooling towers.
misc: The Sun is at a FOCUS of Earth's orbit, not at the centre.
A parabola is not a 'long ellipse' — it never closes.

examples.title: All conics from one equation: sweep the eccentricity
examples.world: The Greeks cut cones; Kepler found the planets on ellipses.

examples.title: Earth's orbit: e = 0.0167, nearly a circle
examples.world: Perihelion 0.983 AU in early January, aphelion 1.017 AU in July.

examples.title: Halley's comet: e = 0.967
examples.world: a ≈ 17.8 AU: it swings in to 0.59 AU from the Sun every ~76 years.

examples.title: The ellipse's second focus: shattering kidney stones
examples.world: An ellipsoidal reflector sends a spark's shock wave from one focus to the stone at the other (extracorporeal lithotripsy).

examples.title: The parabola's focus: a dish antenna
examples.world: Every ray parallel to the axis reflects to the focus, where the feed horn sits.

examples.title: The DNA double helix as a space curve
examples.world: Radius 10 Å, one turn every 34 Å (Watson & Crick 1953); the curvature is constant.

chapters.title: Complex numbers
chapters.what: A complex number z = x + iy is a point of the plane; multiplying by it turns and stretches. e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ turns rotation into algebra.
chapters.looks: A phasor spins in the plane; stacked along time in 3D it becomes a helix whose shadows are the cosine and the sine.
chapters.change: Add a second phasor with a phase shift: the sum is still a sinusoid, with a new amplitude and phase.
chapters.use: AC circuits (phasors), signal processing (FFT), aerodynamics (conformal maps), RF engineering (the Smith chart).
misc: i is not 'imaginary' in the sense of useless: every AC calculation uses it.
There are exactly n n-th roots, evenly spaced on a circle.

examples.title: A rotating phasor and its shadow, the sine wave
examples.world: Steinmetz's phasor method: every AC voltage is the shadow of a rotating arrow.

examples.title: Adding two AC voltages out of phase
examples.world: Two sources of 1 and 0.8 V differing by 1.2 rad give 1.49 V, not 1.8 V.

examples.title: Roots of unity: the FFT's twiddle factors
examples.world: The fast Fourier transform (Cooley & Tukey 1965) is built on the eight 8th roots of 1.

examples.title: Multiplying turns and stretches
examples.world: |zw| = |z||w| and the angles add: 1.5 × 1.2 = 1.8.

examples.title: The Joukowski map turns circles into airfoils
examples.world: w = z + 1/z maps a shifted circle to a wing section; flow round the circle becomes flow round the wing.

examples.title: The Möbius map behind the Smith chart
examples.world: Γ = (z − 1)/(z + 1) maps a line's normalised impedance to its reflection coefficient.
